activities.description: A silhouette of a head is drawn.
A labyrinth fills the head, with a seated figure at the top.
Three circles with text are drawn: "Automatic Reactions & Skills," "Implicit Knowledge," and "Instinct & Intuition."
Text "CONSCIOUS MIND" appears above the seated figure.
Text "SHORTCUT" is written diagonally across the labyrinth, with an arrow pointing towards a globe.
The globe is drawn, with Alice falling through it.
Three flags with text are drawn around the globe.
A flowchart diagram is drawn, with a bottle labeled "DRINK ME."

scenes.contextualRelevance: The use of Alice in Wonderland imagery adds a layer of whimsy and suggests that the unconscious mind operates in a realm of symbolic and imaginative associations.

mood.description: Curious. The animation and narration introduce the concept of the unconscious mind in a visually engaging and intriguing manner.

narrativeProgression.description: The unconscious mind is introduced visually with a labyrinth and a seated figure.
The elements of the unconscious mind are further illustrated: automatic reactions, implicit knowledge, and instinct/intuition.
The unconscious mind's use of shortcuts is explained.
The sources of these shortcuts are depicted: background, cultural environment, and personal experiences.
The result of these shortcuts is illustrated - quick decision-making, symbolized by the flowchart and "DRINK ME" bottle.

props.name: Flags with text and associated images

scenes.thematicElements: Introduction to the unconscious mind, its elements, its working mechanism, and its role in decision-making.
scenes.title: Introduction to the Unconscious Mind

videoEditingDetails.description: Text "THE ROYAL SOCIETY" fades in on a magenta background. The background then lightens to pink.
Animated drawings on a white background.

activities.description: Alice, the Mad Hatter, and the White Rabbit appear at the bottom of the globe.
Text "WRONG!" appears in a speech bubble above Alice.
Text "THIS MATTER NEEDS RATIONAL THINKING" appears in a speech bubble above the Mad Hatter.

characterInteraction.description: The appearance of Alice and the Wonderland characters creates a humorous juxtaposition, suggesting the absurd results that can arise from unconscious biases.

scenes.contextualRelevance: The use of Alice in Wonderland, a story known for its illogical situations, reinforces the idea of flawed unconscious judgments.

mood.description: Confused, Humorous. The scene points out the fallibility of the unconscious mind using a lighthearted example.

narrativeProgression.description: The scene introduces the idea that the unconscious mind's quick decision-making can often be wrong.
It emphasizes that matters needing rational thinking often require conscious, analytical processing.

props.name: Alice, the Mad Hatter, the White Rabbit

scenes.thematicElements: Fallibility of the unconscious mind, the need for rational thinking in specific situations.
scenes.title: Fallibility of the Unconscious Mind

activities.description: The Cricket Player appears, drawing a blackboard with text "A CLASSIC EXAMPLE" and "QUESTION" on it.
He draws a cricket bat, a plus sign, a cricket ball, and writes "£1.10."
He rewrites the equation as "£1 + (cricket ball)."
Text "HOW MUCH DOES THE BALL COST?" appears beside the Cricket Player.
"50%" is written with a globe and stick figures representing students.
Text "OF STUDENTS AT SOME OF THE WORLD'S LEADING UNIVERSITIES GET THE ANSWER..." appears below the globe.
A button with text "WRONG" appears below the previous text.
"10p" is written with a coin.
Text "THE ANSWER IS" appears below the coin.
The Royal Society emblem appears.
Text "5p" appears.
A head silhouette appears on a podium.
The head is filled with an iceberg labeled "UNCONSCIOUS MIND," with the top portion labeled "CONSCIOUS MIND." An arrow labeled "INSTINCT" points from the unconscious mind to the conscious mind.
A thought bubble with "ANALYSIS" appears above the conscious mind.
Text "JUDGEMENT" appears below the podium.
The scene shifts to playing cards, some with King and Queen figures.
The cards are arranged into two groups: "INGROUP" and "OUTGROUP."
A speech bubble "YOU'RE JUST LIKE ME!" appears from a King card to another.

characterInteraction.description: The Cricket Player plays the role of a teacher, challenging viewers with a problem and explaining the concept of unconscious bias.

scenes.contextualRelevance: The bat and ball problem serves as a tangible example of how easily our unconscious mind can mislead us, even in seemingly simple situations.

mood.description: Engaging, Thought-provoking. The scene presents a classic cognitive puzzle, illustrating how unconscious bias can lead to errors in judgment.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Visuals shift from analytical to symbolic, highlighting the role of unconscious judgment.

narrativeProgression.description: Introduction of the classic bat and ball problem.
The surprising statistic of highly educated students getting the answer wrong.
The scene shifts to a visual representation of the unconscious mind's dominance in making judgments.
Introduction of the concept of "INGROUP" and "OUTGROUP" categorization.

scenes.thematicElements: Unconscious bias, instinct vs. analysis, ingroup/outgroup categorization, flawed judgment.
scenes.title: Consequences of Unconscious Bias

activities.description: Text "WE'RE THE WINNING HAND" appears in a speech bubble from a King card to a Queen card in the "INGROUP."
Text "THIS IS A PRIVATE CLUB" appears in a speech bubble from a Queen card to another Queen card in the "INGROUP."
Text "THAT'S UNCONSCIOUS BIAS" appears above the playing cards.
A head silhouette reappears.
Text "BIAS COLOURS OUR DECISIONS WITHOUT OUR REALISING" appears inside the silhouette.
The male symbol appears beside the head.
Text "MALE VOICE" appears below the male symbol.
A pyramid labeled "ROYAL SOCIETY" appears on top of the head.
An award certificate appears above the pyramid.
Various science-related doodles appear around the head, with text labels like "ASTRONAUTILUS," "ELECTRICITY EEL," "SCHRÖDINGER'S CATFISH," "THE UNIVERSE IS BANANAS," etc.
A shark's open mouth appears within the head silhouette.
A figure on a platform appears on the right, speaking in a speech bubble, "BUT THIS IS THE WAY WE'VE ALWAYS DONE IT."
A signpost labeled "DANGER - UNCONSCIOUS BIAS" appears on the right.
Three stick figures appear below the signpost on a small boat, speaking in a speech bubble, "WE'RE GONNA NEED A BIGGER BOAT!"

scenes.contextualRelevance: The shark metaphor symbolizes the destructive potential of unconscious bias, while the small boat with stick figures represents the inadequacy of current efforts to address this issue.

mood.description: Serious, Cautionary. The scene explores the implications of unconscious bias in science, highlighting the need for awareness and mitigation strategies.

keyMoments.changeDescription: The shark's mouth appearing within the head creates a visual sense of danger and urgency, shifting the mood to one of caution.

narrativeProgression.description: Demonstration of how unconscious bias can favor "in-groups," leading to exclusion.
Explicitly naming the phenomenon as "UNCONSCIOUS BIAS."
Asserting that bias unconsciously influences our decisions.
Linking unconscious bias to gender by introducing the "MALE VOICE" concept.
Showing the wide range of talent in science, emphasizing the need for diverse perspectives.
Introducing the threat that unconscious bias poses to achieving excellence in science.
The "DANGER" signpost visually reinforces the potential consequences of ignoring unconscious bias.

scenes.thematicElements: Unconscious bias in science, diversity in STEM, achieving excellence, the need for change.
scenes.title: Implications of Unconscious Bias

activities.description: Text "WE'RE ENCOURAGING PANEL MEMBERS TO:" appears on a white background.
An arrow pointing from "FAST" to "SLOW" appears with text "DELIBERATELY SLOW DOWN DECISION MAKING" below it.
A scale with blocks labeled "A" and "B" appears, with text "RECONSIDER REASONS FOR DECISIONS" below it.
Three stacked books with eyes appear, with text "QUESTION CULTURAL STEREOTYPES" below them.
An iceberg appears with a hand pointing to it, with text "MONITOR EACH OTHER FOR UNCONSCIOUS BIAS" below it.
The full infographic with all previously drawn elements appears for a brief moment.
Two head silhouettes appear on a white background.
The silhouettes come closer together.
The silhouettes merge into a single image within a frame.
The frame shrinks and transforms into a goblet silhouette.

scenes.contextualRelevance: The merging of the head silhouettes into a goblet signifies the potential for achieving a unified perspective and greater understanding through collaborative efforts.

mood.description: Hopeful, Empowering. The scene outlines proactive strategies to mitigate unconscious bias, offering a positive outlook.

keyMoments.changeDescription: The shift to the head silhouettes creates a sense of connection and dialogue, suggesting a positive move towards addressing bias.

narrativeProgression.description: The scene shifts focus from explaining unconscious bias to proposing solutions.
Encouraging deliberate decision-making.
Prompting reconsideration of reasons for decisions.
Advocating for challenging cultural stereotypes.
Promoting mutual monitoring for unconscious bias.

scenes.thematicElements: Mitigating unconscious bias, self-awareness, critical thinking, collective action.
scenes.title: Solutions and Mitigation Strategies

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition from animated drawings to text on a white background.
Brief flash of the entire infographic.
Text "royalsociety.org/diversity" appears on a magenta background.

climax.description: The video highlights the serious implications of unconscious bias on judgment and decision-making, particularly within scientific communities. This culminates in an urgent call for conscious efforts to address and mitigate bias, driving home the video's core message.

storylines.description: The video explores the complexities of the unconscious mind and its influence on judgment, especially in a scientific context. It clarifies the potential dangers of unconscious bias and proposes actionable strategies to mitigate it.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: The unconscious mind is amazing. It can process vastly more information than our conscious
mind by using shortcuts based on our background, cultural environment and personal experiences
to make almost instantaneous decisions about everything around us. The snag is, it's
wrong quite a lot of the time, especially on matters that need rational thinking.
Here's a classic example. A bat and a ball cost £1.10. If the bat costs £1 more than
the ball, how much does the ball cost? Most people, including over 50% of students at some
of the world's leading universities, get the answer wrong and say £10. The answer is
actually £5. Many of us choose £10 without thinking. This is because our unconscious mind
uses instinct, not analysis. So our unconscious is fallible. It's also biased. It makes
snap judgments of people we meet, categorising them according to gender, social and other
characteristics. In milliseconds, we judge whether somebody is like us and belongs to our
in-group. These are the people we favour. So men might favour men while women might
favour women, however we can belong to different in-groups and we like to be part of an in-group
that's powerful, which could mean a woman favouring a man over a woman. That's unconscious
bias. All of us have it and it colours our decisions without our realising. For example,
research reveals that if I were a man, you would be more likely to be nodding in agreement
right now because people pay more attention to a male voice. The Royal Society fosters
excellence in science, but this can only be achieved if we select from the widest range
of talent and that's not possible if unconscious bias is narrowing down the field for non-scientific
reasons. To lessen the impact of unconscious bias, which is easier for us to notice in others,
we are raising the awareness of unconscious bias to members of our selection and appointment
panels. We're encouraging panel members to deliberately slow down decision making, reconsider
reasons for decisions, question cultural stereotypes and monitor each other for unconscious bias.
We can't cure unconscious bias, but with self-awareness we can address it.

youtube_description: This animation introduces the key concepts of unconscious bias.  It forms part of the Royal Society’s efforts to ensure that all those who serve on Royal Society selection and appointment panels are aware of differences in how candidates may present themselves, how to recognise bias in yourself and others, how to recognise inappropriate advocacy or unreasoned judgement. You can find out more about unconscious bias and download a briefing which includes current academic research at www.royalsociety.org/diversity.
